# Discrete 3′ UTR sequence motifs regulate nanos RNA enrichment in Drosophila germ granules

**Authors:** Kira Mitchel; Elizabeth R Gavis

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Molecular Biology, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, 08544, USA

## Abstract

Germ granules are ribonucleoprotein condensates that concentrate key maternal mRNAs needed for germ cell development. In Drosophila, nanos mRNA is selectively enriched in germ granules but the specific cis-acting elements mediating this process remain poorly defined. Here, we identify discrete sequence motifs in the nanos 3′ UTR that regulate nanos enrichment specifically by promoting the growth of homotypic nanos mRNA clusters within granules, without affecting the initial targeting of nanos to germ granules. These sequence motifs are binding sites for the hnRNP M homolog Rumpelstiltskin (Rump) and mutation of Rump binding sites or Rump attenuates nanos homotypic cluster growth, reducing the amount of nanos inherited by germ cells. Consequently, germ cells exhibit defective migration to the gonad. Together, our findings reveal how small repeated sequence motifs and cognate RNA-binding proteins can tune enrichment of germ granule mRNAs by driving self-assembly into large RNA clusters. This strategy ensures sufficient inheritance of mRNAs to support germ cell development and may represent a general mechanism by which ribonucleoprotein condensates regulate transcript dosage.

## Introduction

During embryonic development, two foundational cell populations develop: somatic cells and germ cells. While somatic cells generate the diverse cell types that form the body of an animal, germ cells produce the gametes, which give rise to the next generation. Therefore, specification, maintenance, and protection of the germ cells is a biological imperative. A conserved characteristic of germ cells is the presence of germ granules. Germ granules, a category of ribonucleoprotein (RNP) granules, are repositories for mRNAs and proteins required for germ cell development. Although the timing of germ granule formation varies among species, numerous granule components are conserved across the animal kingdom and are crucial for germ cell development (Pamula and Lehmann, 2024; Strome and Updike, 2015).

In Drosophila, germ granules form at the posterior of the oocyte and persist in the embryo, where they are segregated to the primordial germ cells (called pole cells) (Chen et al., 2025). Drosophila germ granules house maternally provided mRNAs that are synthesized in the ovarian nurse cells and transferred en masse to the oocyte. Cytoplasmic flows circulate incoming maternal mRNAs throughout the oocyte, facilitating contact with nascent germ granule protein scaffolds that are preassembled at the posterior pole, in a cytoplasmic domain called the germ plasm (Becalska and Gavis, 2009; Forrest and Gavis, 2003; Little et al., 2015). Designated mRNAs become incorporated at varying frequencies into the granule protein scaffolds through the activity of localization elements in their 3′ untranslated regions (3′ UTRs) (Eagle et al., 2018; Gavis et al., 1996; Rangan et al., 2009). Within granules, mRNAs recruit like transcripts, forming homotypic clusters—discrete ensembles of RNAs with shared identity (Niepielko et al., 2018; Little et al., 2015; Trcek et al., 2015). Self-recruitment through homotypic clustering drives enrichment of mRNAs necessary for germline development (Niepielko et al., 2018). Notably, this form of RNA self-segregation has subsequently been observed in germline granules in other species (Eno et al., 2019; Parker et al., 2020; Roovers et al., 2018; Scholl et al., 2024; Westerich et al., 2023).

Studies of several key germ granules mRNAs, including nanos, polar granule component (pgc) and germ-cell less (gcl), showed that germ granule 3′ UTRs contain multiple, weak, and partially functionally redundant sequences that collectively promote localization (Eagle et al., 2018; Gavis et al., 1996). Our previous work demonstrated that targeting of mRNAs to granules and homotypic cluster growth within them are governed by distinct classes of 3′ UTR elements (Eagle et al., 2018).

Computational modeling and experimental validation identified a “clustering factor,” a quantifiable parameter that measures the influence of the 3′ UTR specifically on homotypic cluster size (Valentino et al., 2022). However, specific sequence or structural features controlling this parameter remain unidentified. Thus, identification of sequence motifs that fine tune this clustering factor is critical to understanding germ granule mRNA enrichment. Here, we identify discrete, cis-acting sequence motifs that control the enrichment of nanos mRNA in germ granules without affecting nanos targeting. This enrichment is driven by the growth of large homotypic clusters and is mediated by the hnRNP M homolog Rumpelstiltskin (Rump). Decreased cluster growth impairs migration of pole cells to the gonad. Together, our results reveal the central role that small motifs and their cognate binding partners play in controlling localization of germ granule transcripts. This strategy could be leveraged by many types of RNP granules.

## Results

### Discrete sequence motifs mediate nanos enrichment within granules

The nanos 3′ UTR contains four motifs recognized by Drosophila hnRNP M homolog Rump. Two of these Rump binding sites (RBS2 and 3, Fig. 1A) were previously shown to contribute to nanos localization using a sensitized assay and non-quantitative histochemical in situ hybridization that could only detect gross accumulation at the posterior pole of the embryo (Jain and Gavis, 2008). Previous work by high-resolution quantitative confocal imaging revealed that targeting of pgc and gcl to granules and homotypic cluster growth are separable processes mediated by distinct classes of elements within the 3′ UTRs (Eagle et al., 2018). With the ability to discriminate targeting and clustering (enrichment) functions, we reexamined requirements in nanos for these Rump binding sites as well as two nearby Rump binding motifs (RBS1 and 4, Fig. 1A) that were not previously tested. We also tested the requirement for a different motif that is conserved among the nanos, pgc, and gcl 3′ UTRs (CM, Fig. 1A). By a gfp reporter assay, mutation of this motif in the nanos, pgc, or gcl 3′ UTR reduced the number of transcripts that accumulate per granule (Eagle et al., 2018). Unlike the previous studies, we tested the requirements for the Rump binding sites and conserved motif in the context of otherwise wildtype nanos mRNA. To this end, nanos transgenes with the motifs mutated or deleted in varying combinations were generated (Figs. 1A and 2A) and introduced into nanos mRNA-null (nanosBNx) flies so that all nanos mRNA produced in these animals is derived from the transgenes. For all transgenes analyzed, nanos expression levels were equivalent to that of a wildtype (WT) nanos transgene, nanosWT, integrated at the same genomic locus, as confirmed by qRT-PCR (Supplemental Fig. 1A).

To determine if and how the mutations affect targeting and enrichment, we performed single molecule fluorescent in situ hybridization (smFISH) for nanos in late-stage oocytes and quantified: (1) the frequency with which germ granules are populated by nanos (targeting) as measured by colocalization of nanos mRNA with an independent germ marker, CycB mRNA, and (2) the number of nanos mRNA transcripts per granule (enrichment) (Fig. 1B–D, 2B–D). The majority of granules contain a single nanos homotypic cluster; therefore, as before, we infer that number of transcripts per granule reflects homotypic cluster size (Eagle et al., 2018; Niepielko et al., 2018). Because mRNAs populate germ granules independently of one another, localization of CycB is unaffected by changes in nanos localization (Niepielko et al., 2018). As a baseline, with a single copy of the nanosWT transgene, nanos puncta colocalized with CycB puncta at an average frequency of 50% (Fig. 1B and C) and germ granules contained an average of 5 nanos transcripts (Fig. 1B and D).

We first assayed the impact of disrupting all five sites. We generated two nanos mutant transgenes: one in which all four Rump binding sites and the conserved motif were deleted (nanosΔRBS1234,ΔCM) and one in which all 4 Rump binding sites were changed from CGUU to CCUU—which was previously shown to completely disrupt Rump binding in vitro (Jain and Gavis, 2008)—and the conserved motif from CAAGUC to ACCUGA (nanosRBS1234*,CM*). In both cases, colocalization of nanos with CycB was unaffected, indicating that targeting of nanos to germ granules was not impacted (Fig. 1B and C). To confirm that targeting was unaffected, we also quantified colocalization between nanos and pgc, another germ granule mRNA (Supplemental Fig. 1B–C). Consistently, colocalization of nanos with pgc was not affected by the RBS and CM mutations. In contrast to granule colocalization, the average number of nanos transcripts per granule was reduced by ~40% in both nanosΔRBS1234,ΔCM and nanosRBS1234*,CM* oocytes as compared to nanosWT (Fig. 1B and D). Thus, while germ granule recognition by nanos mRNA was unaffected by deletion or disruption of these motifs, enrichment was compromised.

### Rump binding sites, but not the conserved motif, control nanos enrichment

To determine whether the Rump binding sites, the conserved motif, or their combination are the primary contributors to nanos enrichment, we generated nanos transgenes with either all four Rump binding site mutations (nanosRBS1234*) or a complete deletion of the conserved motif (nanosΔCM) (Fig. 2A). The nanosRBS1234* mRNA behaved similarly to nanos transcripts with both the Rump binding site and conserved motif mutations: colocalization of nanosRBS1234* with CycB was unaffected, but there was a ~40% reduction in the average number of mRNAs per granule (Fig. 2B–D; compare Fig. 1C and D to Fig. 2C and D). By contrast, localization of nanosΔCM mRNA was indistinguishable from that of nanosWT (Fig. 2B–D). This finding suggests that the Rump binding sites, and not the conserved motif, are the primary drivers of nanos cluster growth. We note that a second copy of the conserved motif is present in a region of the nanos 3′ UTR that is entirely dispensable for nanos localization. Both copies of the motif were mutated in the reporter assay previously used to test localization function; therefore, we cannot rule out the possibility that although the second copy does not impact nanos localization on its own, the two can act redundantly or that the conserved motif might act redundantly with other undefined elements in the nanos transcript.

We then tested whether the number of Rump binding sites matters by generating nanos transgenes with 2 (nanosRBS13*) or 3 (nanosRBS134* and nanosRBS124*) of the four sites mutated. All transgenes behaved similarly to nanosRBS1234* (Fig. 2B–D). The finding that restoring one or two Rump binding sites (compare nanosRBS13* and nanosRBS134* or nanosRBS124* and nanosRBS1234*) did not increase the number of nanos transcripts per granule suggests that the motifs do not influence nanos cluster growth in a scalable fashion. To rule out the possibility that RBS1—which is mutated in all the transgenes—is the only required RBS, we assayed nanos targeting and enrichment in nanosΔ97–147, which removes RBS2 and RBS3 while leaving RBS1 intact. Indeed, targeting of nanosΔ97–147 mRNA was unaffected, while mRNA enrichment was decreased more than 30% as compared to nanosWT mRNA levels (Fig. 2B–D). We conclude that no specific Rump binding site is required and that the motifs act equivalently. Moreover, disruption of any two Rump binding sites is sufficient to impair nanos enrichment in germ granules. Collectively, these results demonstrate that the Rump binding sites facilitate nanos enrichment.

The enrichment of nanos in germ granules is dosage dependent. Whereas the frequency of germ granule colocalization is minimally affected when the quantity of nanos in the oocyte is halved or doubled, the number of nanos transcripts per granule is decreased or increased, respectively (Niepielko et al., 2018). We reasoned that increasing the total amount of mutant nanos mRNA in the oocyte by using two copies of each transgene might restore the enrichment of nanos in granules to wildtype levels. For all mutants, adding a second copy of the transgene increased the average number of nanos transcripts per granule from 3 to 4 (Supplemental Fig. 1D and F; Supplemental Fig. 2A and C) but was less effective than even a single copy of nanosWT (5 mRNA/granule; compare Fig. 1D to Supplemental Fig. 1F and Supplemental Fig. 2C). Thus, without the Rump binding sites, enrichment of nanos mRNA is dampened even in the presence of higher total nanos levels, supporting that transcript enrichment relies specifically on the interactions mediated by the Rump binding sites.

### Rump binding sites specifically control nanos homotypic cluster growth

The quantity of nanos varies among individual granules, ranging from a single transcript to clusters containing as many as 40 transcripts in oocytes with one copy of the nanosWT transgene and up to 80 transcripts in oocytes with two copies (Little et al., 2015) (Supplemental Fig. 3A and B). To gain further insight into how RBS mutations affect nanos enrichment, we quantified the effect of the mutations on the nanos cluster size (number of transcripts) distribution. For each oocyte, we detected all nanos-containing puncta in the germ plasm and binned them by size. The percentage of all puncta in the germ plasm represented by each bin was then averaged for all oocytes within each genotype (Fig. 3A). As expected, nanosWT and nanosΔCM clusters had very similar size distributions. For all RBS mutants, however, there was a marked shift toward smaller cluster sizes as compared to nanosWT. Approximately 75% of granules in RBS mutant oocytes contained 4 or fewer nanos transcripts as compared to 55% in nanosWT oocytes (Fig. 3A). In contrast, only 5%-10% of granules in RBS mutants contained more than 8 nanos transcripts, compared to 20% of granules in nanosWT oocytes (Fig. 3A). Finally, while 5% of nanosWT granules had more than 16 transcripts, few, if any, granules in RBS mutants reached this quantity (Fig. 3A). A similar trend was observed for oocytes with two copies of a nanos mutant transgene, with a decrease in large clusters and an increase in smaller clusters (Supplemental Fig. 3C). These data suggest that RBS mutant nanos transcripts are less effective at building clusters above a particular size. Moreover, they are consistent with the contribution of Rump binding sites to enrichment of nanos in, but not its targeting to, germ granules (Fig. 1B–D, Fig. 2B–D).

*Fig. 3.: Rump binding sites direct nanos cluster growth.(A) Histogram showing the distribution of nanos mRNA cluster sizes for oocytes with one copy of a nanos transgene, binned as indicated, and averaged for all oocytes quantified. For each oocyte, each granule (puncta detected) was re-categorized as containing greater than (large, B) or fewer than (small, C) 8 transcripts. To determine how large and small clusters contributed to the total localized transcript population within a given oocyte (transcript contribution), the number of transcripts per granule for all “small” granules or for all “large” granules was summed and divided by the total number of transcripts within that oocyte. (D) Percent transcript loss was calculated using a percent change formula. For all graphs, mean ± SEM is shown; n = 4–12 oocytes. n. s. = not significant, ****p < 0.0001 as determined by ordinary one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test.*

We next speculated that germ granules containing larger numbers of nanos mRNAs might contribute disproportionately to the quantity of nanos delivered to the pole cells. To evaluate the contribution of these larger clusters to the quantity of localized nanos, we regrouped the granules into two categories: granules with clusters containing fewer than 8 transcripts (“small”) or granules with clusters containing 8 or more transcripts (“large”) (Fig. 3B and C). A cut-off of 8 transcripts was chosen because, on average, 95% of germ granule for RBS nanos mutants have fewer than 8 transcripts (Fig. 3A). In nanosWT and nanosΔCM oocytes, granules containing large clusters account for 20% of the total granule population yet they contribute over 50% of the nanos transcripts in the germ plasm (Fig. 3A and B). This disproportionate contribution by large granules is lost in the RBS mutants. For the remaining 6 mutants, 5–10% of transcripts reside in large clusters and these in turn contribute 5–15% (4 mutants) or 20–30% (2 mutants) of nanos in the germ plasm (Fig. 3A and B). We observed a similar trend with two copies of the transgenes (Supplemental Fig. 3C–E). Thus, although they are the minority, granules with large clusters make the greatest contribution to localized nanos mRNA.

To demonstrate definitively that the contribution of large clusters is integral to amassing nanos, we evaluated the consequence of failing to generate large clusters by RBS mutants. All mutants, regardless of transgene copy number, have 25–40% less nanos in the germ plasm as compared to wildtype (Fig. 3D, Supplemental Fig. 3F). Together, these results show that RBS mutations compromise the ability to generate large nanos mRNA clusters and, consequently, decrease the quantity of nanos mRNA in the germ plasm.

### Reducing nanos enrichment adversely impacts germ cell migration

Across species, Nanos protein suppresses the somatic program and is indispensable for germ cell development. Drosophila germ cells lacking Nanos fail to migrate to the gonad and undergo apoptosis (Asaoka et al., 1998; Deshpande et al., 1999; Hayashi et al., 2004; Lai et al., 2012). Swapping the nanos 3′ UTR with 3′ UTRs from nanos orthologs in other Drosophila species severely reduces nanos enrichment and results in defects in pole cell migration (Doyle et al., 2023). Therefore, we hypothesized that the reduced enrichment of nanos due to RBS mutations would lead to a reduction in Nanos protein and consequently an increase in the number of pole cells that fail to reach the gonad (“lost pole cells”).

To investigate the effect of RBS mutations on nanos function in pole cells, we visualized pole cells in either nanosWT and nanosΔRBS1234,ΔCM embryos at stage 14–15, when they have coalesced in the gonad, with an antibody to the germ cell marker Vasa (Liu et al., 2003) (Fig. 4A and B). In nanosΔRBS1234,ΔCM embryos, there is a higher frequency of lost pole cells than in nanosWT (Fig. 4B). Thus, disruptions to the Rump binding sites and the consequent loss in nanos enrichment results in downstream defects in pole cell development.

*Fig. 4.: Loss of Rump binding sites impairs embryonic development.(A) Vasa, detected by anti-Vasa immunohistochemistry, marks the pole cells in Bownes staged 14–15 embryos with one copy of transgenic nanos. Arrows indicate pole cells that did not complete their migration to the gonad (“lost pole cells”). (B) Percentage of embryos with the indicated number of lost pole cells; n = 417 embryos for nanosWT and 143 embryos for nanosΔ1234,ΔCM.*

### Rump is required specifically for nanos enrichment

The disruption of nanos enrichment caused by RBS mutations predicts that loss of Rump should have a similar effect. To determine if Rump controls nanos cluster size, we performed smFISH to detect nanos in either control or rump mutant oocytes expressing the germ granule marker Oskar-sfGFP (Fig. 5A). Quantification of colocalization between nanos and Oskar-sfGFP showed that, consistent with the behavior of the RBS mutants, mRNA targeting was not impacted by loss of Rump (Fig. 5B). Control (oskar-sfgfp) oocytes accumulated ~9 nanos transcripts per granule, whereas rump mutant oocytes had approximately a third fewer nanos transcripts per granule. Thus, eliminating Rump is sufficient to reduce cluster size and suggests that Rump may play a role in nanos enrichment.

(B) Nearest-neighbor colocalization quantification of the experiment in (A). (C) Quantification of the average number of nanos RNAs per granule. Individual data points represent the mean value for one oocyte. For both (B) and (C) mean ± SEM are shown; n = 10 to 11 oocytes. n.s. = not significant,**p < 0.005 as determined by an unpaired t-test. (D) Visualization of the entire germ plasm in 30 μm z-series projections of oskar-sfgfp and oskar-sfgfp; rump– stage 13 oocytes. (E) Quantification of total Oskar-sfGFP fluorescence intensity. Each sample was normalized to that sample’s total CycB fluorescence intensity. Mean ± SEM are shown; n = 4 to 5 oocytes. n.s. = not significant by a Welch’s t-test. Data points from three experimental replicate blots (Fig. 5F and Supplemental Fig. 4G), mean ± SD is shown; n. s. = not significant by a Mann-Whitney test. Scale bars = 20 μm.*

Sequence analysis of two other germ granule mRNAs, pgc and CycB, revealed that both contain putative Rump binding sites (5 and 2, respectively). Rump could therefore regulate other germ granule mRNAs in addition to nanos. To test this possibility, we detected pgc and CycB together with Oskar-sfGFP in control and rump mutant oocytes (Supplemental Fig. 4A and B). However, neither targeting nor enrichment of either mRNA was affected in rump mutant oocytes (Supplemental Fig. 4D–F). Therefore, Rump’s role in promoting cluster growth is likely specific to nanos.

Mutations in numerous genes cause defects in localization of germ granule mRNAs because of their requirement for local production of the germ granule organizer Oskar. Previously, we showed that Oskar levels are unaffected in rump mutant embryos (Jain and Gavis, 2008). To confirm that this is also the case in oocytes, we imaged Oskar-sfGFP in late-stage control and rump mutant oocytes. (Fig. 5D). Fluorescence intensity quantification showed that Oskar-sfGFP levels were unaffected in rump mutant oocytes (Fig. 5E). Western blot analysis of Oskar showed that while total Oskar levels vary between oskar-sfgfp and oskar-sfgfp; rump– oocytes, the total amount of Oskar in oskar-sfgfp; rump– oocytes (wildtype Oskar plus Oskar-sfGFP) is not significantly different from the total amount of Oskar in wildtype oocytes (Fig. 5G, Supplemental Fig. 4G). Furthermore, if there were significant changes to Oskar levels in oskar-sfgfp; rump– oocytes, we would expect to a decrease in CycB and pgc localization, which is not observed (Supplemental Fig. 4A–F). Collectively, these data indicate that Rump plays a role in nanos localization independently of an effect on Oskar.

## Discussion

Targeting of mRNAs to Drosophila germ granules and their enrichment within granules by homotypic clustering are separable functions conferred by 3′ UTRs. However, the precise 3′ UTR features—structures and/or sequences—that mediate these functions have remained elusive. Here, we show that discrete sequence motifs in the nanos 3′ UTR that are recognized by RNA-binding protein Rump specifically regulate the growth of homotypic clusters. Mutating these motifs or rump attenuates cluster growth, implicating Rump as an important mediator of nanos enrichment. Despite the presence of putative Rump binding sites in pgc and CycB mRNAs, Rump does not direct their localization, suggesting that Rump specifically regulates nanos.

Rump-dependent enrichment is crucial to maximize the inheritance of nanos by pole cells and ensure robust germline development. Mutation of two, three, or four Rump binding sites similarly reduced nanos enrichment, implying that at least two Rump binding sites must be unaltered for wildtype localization. However, no particular combination of sites appears to be critical. Repeated motifs frequently act redundantly to each other (Herve et al., 2004). For example, translational repression of unlocalized nanos mRNA is conferred by either of two binding sites for the Smaug repressor in the nanos 3′ UTR (Smibert et al., 1996). By contrast, here we show that multiple, identical motifs must be present to mediate nanos enrichment.

Consistent with the behavior of RBS mutants, nanos cluster size alone is reduced in rump mutant oocytes. Rump is enriched in nurse cell nuclei, where nanos is first transcribed, but does not accumulate at the posterior of early embryos (Jain and Gavis, 2008), suggesting that Rump binds to nanos prior to its export to the cytoplasm and does not remain stably associated with nanos once integrated into germ granules. However, Rump co-immunoprecipitates with the core granule proteins Oskar and Aubergine (Aub), supporting at least a transient interaction with germ granules (Becalska et al., 2011; Hurd et al., 2016). Because it contains three RNA Recognition Motifs (RRMs) (Geuens et al., 2016; Jain and Gavis, 2008), Rump could engage multiple nanos mRNAs simultaneously. This multivalency may allow Rump bound to one nanos to interact transiently with additional clustered nanos transcripts through its remaining RRMs. We therefore propose that Rump mediates a hand-off of nanos transcripts to growing nanos clusters within germ granules via multivalent RNA-binding and interactions with granule proteins such as Oskar and Aub. Once Rump has transferred nanos to a cluster, it dissociates, explaining its lack of posterior accumulation (Jain and Gavis, 2008).

Rump binding sites facilitate the assembly of higher copy nanos clusters that contribute a substantial fraction of the total amount of nanos in the germ plasm. Homotypic clustering likely stabilizes and retains mRNAs within germ granules, driving their accumulation in the germ plasm (Niepielko et al., 2018). In vitro RNA clusters formed by homotypic RNA-RNA interactions solidify overtime (Mahendran et al., 2025). Thus, by enhancing nanos cluster growth, nanos-Rump interactions, mediated by Rump binding sites, provide a mechanism by which germ granules effectively “trap” RNAs in stable assemblies. Accordingly, RBS mutations reduce delivery of nanos to pole cells, leading to insufficient Nanos protein, incomplete repression of somatic fate in pole cells, and impaired germ cell migration. These findings indicate that condensate function is sensitive to the efficiency of RNA clustering. Together, our results illustrate how biomolecular condensates can regulate the quantity of their constituent components.

Cluster growth is not abolished entirely in RBS mutants, however, indicating that additional mechanisms initiate clustering. Homotypic RNA-RNA interactions could suffice to nucleate a cluster. Alternatively, or in addition, other cis-acting elements and RBPs may contribute to this process. Rump-dependent interactions likely build on this initial network to promote formation of large clusters needed to ensure proper germ cell development.

## Methods

### Drosophila strains and genetics

The following Drosophila melanogaster strains were used: y1 w67c23 (Bloomington Stock Center 6599); osk-sfgfp (Eichler et al., 2023); rump1 (Jain and Gavis, 2008).The nanosBNx allele was generated by imprecise excision of the w+P element insertion in the original nanosBN chromosome (Wang et al., 1994). The P element is inserted in the nanos 5′ UTR, 262 base pairs upstream of the start codon, and the excision removes a portion of the P element containing the mini-white marker.

### Transgene construction

The wildtype nanos transgene was generated by inserting a 4.3-kb genomic nanos rescue fragment (Gavis and Lehmann, 1992) into the pattB vector (Bischof et al., 2013). For the nanos RBS/CM mutant transgenes, nanos 3′ UTR sequences with the various mutations/deletions were synthesized (Azenta Life Sciences/Genewiz for nanosRBS13* and nanosRBS134* constructs and Twist Bioscience for all others). The mutated nanos 3′ UTR sequences were used to replace the 3′ UTR of the wildtype nanos transgene. The nanos97–147 transgene was generated by deleting nucleotides 97–147 of the nanos 3′ UTR from the wildtype transgene. Transgenes were integrated into the attP40 site by phiC31-mediated recombination (Rainbow Transgenic Flies, Inc for nanosRBS13* and nanosRBS134* transgenes; BestGene, Inc for all other transgenes) and then introduced into a nanosBNx background, which lacks maternal nanos mRNA.

### RNA extraction and RT-qPCR

Females were fed for 2 days at 25 °C on corn meal agar supplemented with ample yeast paste. Ovaries were dissected in PBS, flash frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80 °C. RNA was extracted using the RNeasy kit with DNase digestion (Qiagen). 1 μg total RNA was used to generate cDNA using the Quantitect RT kit (Qiagen). qPCR was performed as previously described (Eichler et al., 2020) using Taqman Gene Expression Assay probes for rpl7 (Thermo Fisher, Dm01817653_g1) and for nanos (Thermo Fisher, Dm02134535_g1) on an Applied Biosystems Step One machine. Each genotype was assayed in at least three biological replicates, with three technical replicates. Relative fold change in gene expression was calculated using −ΔΔCt, using rpl7 as the internal gene control and nanosWT as gene of comparison (Livak and Schmittgen, 2001).

### Single molecule fluorescent in situ hybridization (smFISH)

Ovaries were isolated as described above and smFISH was performed as previously described (Abbaszadeh and Gavis, 2016; Niepielko et al., 2018). Briefly, ovaries were fixed in 4% EM-grade PFA for 30 min, rinsed in PBST, (PBS, 0.1% Tween-20) dehydrated stepwise into methanol, and stored at −20 °C. Ovaries were rehydrated into PBST and incubated in wash buffer for 10 min on a nutator. Probes for nanos and CycB were diluted in hybridization buffer and applied to ovaries at 37 °C for 16 h. Ovaries were washed twice for 30 min intervals at 37 °C with wash buffer, rinsed in PBST, and then stained with DAPI (1.25 μg/mL) and washed 5x in PBST. Ovarioles were separated with fine needles and mounted in Prolong Diamond Antifade Mountant (Invitrogen) between two #1.5 coverslips.

### Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining

Embryos were collected at 25 °C for 6 h and then aged for 20 h at 18 °C. IHC was performed as previously described (Eichler et al., 2020) using rabbit anti-phospho-Vas (1:500, gift of T. Schüpbach) and biotin goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody (1:500, Jackson Immuno Research Laboratories). Embryos were mounted in 80% glycerol under a #1 coverslip. Pole cells were counted using a Zeiss compound light microscope.

### Immunoblotting and quantification

To enrich for late-stage oocytes, osk-sfgfp and osk-sfgfp; rump1 flies were fed for three days, then transferred to empty food vials with wet kimwipes overnight. Dissected ovaries were flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. Oocytes were thawed on ice and homogenized in 2x protein sample buffer (0.125 M Tris-HCl pH 8; 4% SDS; 20% glycerol; 0.1 M DTT; 0.01% bromophenol blue) and boiled for 5 min. Samples were spun in a microfuge at top speed for 10 min and the supernatant was run on a 10% SDS-PAGE gel. Proteins were transferred to nitrocellulose, blocked in Blotto (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5; 150 mM NaCl; 0.1% Tween-20; 5% non-fat dry milk), and then incubated in primary antibody diluted in Blotto overnight at 4 °C with rocking. After washing in Blotto, blots were incubated in secondary antibody diluted in Blotto, at room temperature with rocking for 2 h. Blots were washed with TBST (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5; 150 mM NaCl; 0.1% Tween-20), incubated with Lumi-LightPLUS Western Blotting Substrate (Roche) for 3 min, and imaged using the iBright FL1000 Imaging System (Thermo Fisher). Primary antibodies: 1:20,000 anti-Khc (Cytoskeleton); 1:2500 anti-Oskar (gift of A. Ephrussi). Secondary antibody: 1:2000 HRP rabbit anti-donkey IgG (VWR).

Western blot images were quantified in FIJI (Schindelin et al., 2012). Blots were color-inverted and integrated density was measured for the background and each band on the blot. Background density was subtracted. For each lane, the total relative Oskar level was calculated as the sum of the endogenous Oskar and Oskar-sfGFP density values divided by the density of the loading control (Khc).

### Confocal microscopy

Confocal images of stage 13 oocytes were acquired on a Leica SP5 laser scanning microscope using a 63x 1.4 NA oil immersion objective with 1.5× zoom, and GaAsP “HyD” detectors in photon counting mode. 5 μm z-stacks were taken just below the posterior cortex, using a step size of 340 nm, a frame average of 2, and a line accumulation of 6. All imaging conditions were consistent between genotypes, except for the experiment in Fig. 5D. For imaging of Osk protein in osk-sfgfp and osk-sfgfp; rump1, z-stacks were 30 μm with a step size of 2 μm, a frame average of 2, and a line accumulation of 2.

### Image quantification and statistical analysis

Image quantification methods used have been described in depth previously (Little et al., 2015; Niepielko et al., 2018). Briefly, a custom Matlab (MathWorks) program was used to measure colocalization of nanos mRNA with an independent germ granule marker (e.g., CycB) and the number of nanos mRNAs per granule. The frequency (percent) of colocalization (targeting) was quantified using the Inter-Point Distance Matrix Matlab program with the requirement that two puncta be located within 200 nm in x-y to qualify as residing in the same granule. The number of RNA transcripts contained within each granule (enrichment) was quantified by comparing the fluorescence intensity of puncta in the germ plasm to the fluorescence intensity of puncta in the mid region of the oocyte, which contain single nanos transcripts (Little et al., 2015) and the average number of transcripts per germ granule for each oocyte was obtained using Microsoft Excel “AVERAGEIF” formula, filtering out all values less than 1 (as they would correspond to less than a single RNA transcript). Statistical analysis was performed in Graphpad Prism. Specific statistical tests and p-values are indicated in the figure legends. FIJI was used to quantify the total Oskar fluorescence in Fig. 5E. Z projections were generated using the “sum slices” function for each channel (Oskar and CycB) and the threshold was adjusted to only include localized signal. Integrated Density (total fluorescent signal) was measured. For each oocyte, Oskar fluorescence was normalized to CycB fluorescence.

The histograms, “transcript contribution,” and “% change” analyses were performed in R. To curate the data required for the histograms, we binned puncta: 1, 2–4, 5–8, 9–16, or 17+ transcripts per puncta. The percentage of total punctae represented by each category was then calculated. This value was then averaged across oocytes for each genotype. For transcript contribution, we summed the value of puncta together for puncta with ≤8 transcripts and puncta with >8 transcripts. The percentage of transcript contribution was calculated by dividing each summed value by the total and multiplying by 100. To calculate “% transcript loss,” we used the percent change formula. We subtracted the overall average nanosWT RNA/granule from the average number of RNAs/granule from each oocyte and divided by the overall average nanosWT RNA/granule.
